structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, a principle that has made him a confidant to others but left him disillusioned after returning from the East, where he witnessed moral chaos among the privileged—except for Jay Gatsby, whom he admires for his extraordinary gift for hope and romantic sensitivity. In the spring of 1922, Nick moves to West Egg and rents a modest eighty-dollar-a-month bungalow near the water, sandwiched between two enormous estates, including Gatsby’s mansion; after feeling lonely until a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village, he drives by car across the bay to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, where he meets Jordan Baker and is struck by Tom’s domineering presence and racist views from 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires.' During dinner, a phone call reveals Tom’s affair in New York, which everyone ignores, while Daisy confides in Nick that she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool,' exposing her deep cynicism; later, as Nick drives home to West Egg, he sees Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light across the bay, trembling in the night before vanishing without speaking.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where Tom forcibly pulls him from the train to meet Myrtle Wilson, wife of the pale and anaemic garage owner George Wilson, beneath the looming eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg; Myrtle and Tom arrange to meet in New York, where Myrtle buys a $10 Airedale puppy at a street vendor’s cart before boarding a lavender taxicab with Nick and Tom to her cluttered, oversized-furnished apartment on 158th Street; there, Myrtle calls her sister Catherine and the photographer Mr. McKee and his wife, serves whisky, changes into a cream chiffon dress, and becomes increasingly theatrical and drunk, recounting her intoxicating first meeting with Tom on a train and falsely claiming Daisy is Catholic to justify their planned divorces; the atmosphere grows chaotic until Myrtle defiantly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose with a single blow, after which blood covers the bathroom floor as guests scramble in confusion, Mr. McKee dazedly exits, and Nick departs alone, eventually finding himself exhausted and isolated in the cold, dim interior of Pennsylvania Station at dawn.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The drunken man with owl-eyed spectacles
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick, receiving a formal invitation to attend one of Jay Gatsby’s extravagant Saturday evening parties at his West Egg mansion, where guests arrive by car and train, flooding the grounds with music, dancing on canvas platforms, swimming from rafts, and consuming vast quantities of food and drink prepared by eight servants who repair the damage each Monday—including processing hundreds of oranges daily. Amid the chaotic revelry, Nick overhears wild rumors about Gatsby—such as that he killed a man or was a German spy—and encounters eccentric figures like the drunken man with owl-eyed spectacles, who is astonished to find Gatsby’s library books are real and uncut; he bonds with Jordan Baker and a war veteran who invites him to fly in a newly purchased hydroplane, yet never meets Gatsby until late in the night, when Gatsby reveals himself unexpectedly at a table, warmly invites Nick to fly with him the next morning at nine, and leaves a deep impression with his rare, reassuring smile. As the party descends into chaos—with a weeping chorus girl, couples fighting, wives being forcibly removed, and a new coupé crashing into a wall with Owl Eyes and another man insisting they weren’t driving—Jordan is called away by Gatsby for a private hour-long conversation, leaving Nick alone until he stumbles upon the accident scene; finally, Gatsby stands solitary on his porch, waving farewell as the moon shines over the now-quiet estate. Later, Nick reflects on his daily routine walking to the Probity Trust in lower Manhattan, lunches with clerks, and evening study sessions at the Yale Club, romanticizing strangers on Fifth Avenue at twilight while observing the loneliness of young clerks; he rekindles his acquaintance with Jordan Baker, becoming aware of her dishonesty after learning she lied about damaging a borrowed car and cheated in a major golf tournament, and is unsettled yet allured by her belief that others must avoid her reckless driving, ultimately resolving to end his weekly love letters to a woman back home and affirming his personal honesty.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, coastal church bells ring as a chaotic crowd of guests—drawn from East Egg, West Egg, and New York—floods Gatsby’s mansion in cars, engaging in revelry and gossip; Nick Carraway recalls names from a disintegrating timetable dated July 5th, 1922, listing dozens of attendees including the Snells, Dancies, Klipspringer (known as 'the boarder'), Benny McClenahan with his ever-changing group of girls, and the mysterious 'Duke,' while noting tragic fates like Snell being run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s automobile and Henry L. Palmetto’s suicide. Later, on a late July morning, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, invites him to lunch, and during the drive reveals an elaborate but inconsistent personal history—including inheritance from San Francisco parents, Oxford education, wartime heroism in the Argonne Forest, and a Montenegrin medal for valor—backed by physical proof, while a policeman lets him pass after recognizing a white card, implying elite connections. At noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsheim, a man with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and admits to fixing the 1919 World Series; Gatsby abruptly leaves mid-meal to make a phone call, and when Nick Carraway introduces him to Tom Buchanan, Gatsby vanishes. In a reflective interlude, Jordan Baker recalls meeting Daisy Fay in Louisville in October 1917, seated in a white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby, whose intense gaze left a lasting impression; she later remembers Daisy’s drunken wedding day in June 1919, clutching a letter and a three-hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar pearl necklace before marrying Tom Buchanan, whose scandalous car crash with a chambermaid in Santa Barbara preceded Daisy’s emotional recognition of Gatsby’s name six weeks prior. Finally, at twilight in Central Park, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy and asks him to invite Daisy to tea so Gatsby can visit her unannounced, a modest request after five years of quiet observation, prompting Nick Carraway to shift focus from Gatsby and Daisy to Jordan’s poise, reflecting on the phrase: 'There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.'

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy afternoon in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion unnaturally lit and Gatsby himself awkwardly inviting him to Coney Island and hinting at a side business opportunity. The next day, Nick invites Daisy to tea, explicitly warning her not to bring Tom; as heavy rain falls, Gatsby sends a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers. Daisy arrives by large open car with her chauffeur Ferdie, and Gatsby enters the house pale and trembling. Their reunion is strained—marked by nervous silences and a near-accident with a mantelpiece clock—but after Nick briefly leaves them alone, they emerge transformed: Daisy tear-streaked, Gatsby radiant. When the rain stops, Gatsby joyfully leads Daisy on a tour of his mansion through the big postern, where she admires the feudal silhouette, gardens fragrant with jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate, though the house is eerily silent despite his claims of constant guests. Inside, they pass Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, encountering only Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas doing liver exercises, before Gatsby displays his vast collection of expensive, monogrammed shirts in silk, linen, and flannel, causing Daisy to collapse in tears. Gatsby then shows her a photograph of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful portrait of himself in yachting gear, shares newspaper clippings about her, and takes a frustrated call about a man from Detroit. As the storm clears, Daisy marvels at the pink and golden clouds over the sea, whimsically wishing to put Gatsby inside one; Klipspringer is summoned to play piano, performing 'The Love Nest' and 'The Rich Get Richer' reluctantly before Gatsby commands him to continue. In the dimly lit music room, Gatsby lights Daisy’s cigarette with a trembling match and sits with her in shadow, emotionally reconnected, while Nick observes Gatsby’s growing doubt that reality can match his idealized vision of her. Nick departs as Gatsby and Daisy become fully absorbed in each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement about rumors linking him to underground activities, confirming the wild legends surrounding Gatsby’s persona, including claims he lives in a moving house-boat. The narrative then traces Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, changed his name after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht anchored off Lake Superior; he worked aboard Cody’s Tuolomee for five years in roles including steward, mate, and jailor, absorbing luxury and discipline while developing an aversion to alcohol from witnessing Cody’s excesses. After Cody’s death—following manipulation by Ella Kaye that denied Gatsby his $25,000 inheritance—he retained only the refined identity of Jay Gatsby, forged through years of dreaming and service on the yacht’s coastal journeys. Later, after a weeks-long absence, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled by the unexpected arrival of Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists on offering drinks but is coldly dismissed, especially when Sloane subtly blocks him from joining their ride home. That same Saturday night, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is initially enchanted by the spectacle but becomes increasingly unsettled by the raw, chaotic energy of West Egg’s new rich crowd; Gatsby watches her closely, desperately hoping she will renounce Tom and declare she never loved him, but she is alienated by the party’s vulgarity. Alone with Nick Carraway that night, Gatsby insists Daisy didn’t enjoy the party and reveals his obsessive dream of reversing time to recreate the exact moment five years prior when he kissed her under the moonlight.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting; Gatsby has replaced all original servants with strangers to conceal Daisy’s frequent visits. During a stifling lunch, Daisy openly declares her love for Gatsby in front of Tom, triggering a violent confrontation in which Tom mocks Gatsby’s Oxford claim and reveals he has investigated Gatsby’s past as a bootlegger tied to Meyer Wolfsheim. The group drives to New York City in a volatile car arrangement—Tom takes Gatsby’s yellow car with Nick and Jordan, while Gatsby and Daisy follow in Tom’s coupé—before retreating to a stifling suite at the Plaza Hotel, where Daisy’s wavering confession that she once loved Tom but now loves Gatsby shatters Gatsby’s idealized vision. Tom orders them to return home in Gatsby’s car, effectively ending the confrontation. Meanwhile, Myrtle Wilson, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife and desperate to escape her husband, rushes out of the garage in the Valley of Ashes and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees the scene; Michaelis witnesses the accident but cannot confirm the car’s color. Later, Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Myrtle’s body under a swinging yellow bulb, Wilson hysterical, and Tom denies ownership of the yellow car while whispering to Nick that the driver is a 'God damned coward.' Afterward, Nick leaves the Buchanans’ house alone and finds Gatsby waiting in the drive, who confesses Daisy was driving when Myrtle died and insists he will take the blame; Nick secretly observes Daisy and Tom sitting together quietly in the kitchen, sharing food and ale, revealing their reconciliation, while Gatsby remains outside in the moonlight, vigilantly watching over a house where his dream has already ended.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway finds Gatsby dejected after waiting all night for Daisy, who briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light; they wander through Gatsby’s dusty mansion, disturbing a ghostly piano, and Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee, but he refuses, clinging to the belief that Daisy never truly loved Tom. Gatsby recounts his past: as a penniless officer, he deceived Daisy into believing he was of her social class, fell deeply in love with her during a final afternoon together before his deployment to Oxford—where he was mistakenly sent after the war—and upon returning to find her married, traveled by day-coach to Louisville, walking the streets where they once met, haunted by the memory of leaving her behind. On the same morning, Gatsby puts on his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, and goes alone to the pool, instructing the butler to forward any calls—none come, and he seems to have lost faith in his dream. Later, George Wilson, consumed by grief and delusion after Myrtle’s death, travels on foot from his garage to West Egg, having learned Gatsby’s name, and shoots him in the pool before taking his own life; Nick Carraway arrives to find Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress amid leaves and ripples, while Wilson’s corpse lies in the grass nearby.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: In the aftermath of Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the chaotic scene at Gatsby’s mansion as police, reporters, and curious onlookers swarm the property, while Catherine denies any connection between Myrtle and Gatsby, shaping the narrative as a madman’s crime. Desperate to notify Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim, Nick Carraway makes repeated phone calls and sends a letter via the butler, but receives no response—only a mistaken long-distance call from Chicago that forces him to bluntly announce Gatsby’s death. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and overwhelmed, clutching a worn photograph of the mansion and a tattered childhood schedule of self-improvement, revealing his profound pride in his son’s rise. Despite Nick Carraway’s efforts, only Gatz, the minister, servants, and the postman attend the funeral; Klipspringer declines due to a picnic, and Wolfsheim refuses outright, citing a personal rule against involvement after death. In the rain, an unexpected figure—the man with owl-eyed glasses—appears at the cemetery, wiping rain from his glasses to view Gatsby’s grave, murmuring 'Amen to that' and lamenting the absence of mourners who once filled Gatsby’s parties. Afterward, Nick Carraway reflects on his Western roots through memories of Christmas train rides to Chicago, realizing he and his circle—Tom, Daisy, Jordan, Gatsby—are all displaced Westerners ill-suited to the East’s moral decay, symbolized by a hallucinatory El Greco-like vision of West Egg where a drunken woman lies ignored on a stretcher. He confronts Jordan Baker, who accuses him of dishonesty and reveals she is engaged to another man, leaving him angry, half in love, and deeply sorry. Finally, encountering Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, Nick Carraway learns Tom told Wilson that Gatsby owned the car, justifying it as self-defense while emotionally performing grief over dog biscuits, prompting Nick Carraway to recognize Tom and Daisy as careless people who destroy lives and retreat into wealth. The chapter ends with Nick Carraway visiting Gatsby’s abandoned mansion at night, erasing an obscene word scrawled on the steps, walking to the beach, and meditating on Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light and humanity’s endless struggle against time: 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, Long Island, seeking opportunity in the bond business and renting a modest home next to the lavish mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, arrogant residents of East Egg—Nick is introduced to the hedonistic world of the Jazz Age elite. He also meets Jordan Baker, a cynical professional golfer, and becomes fascinated by Gatsby’s enigmatic persona: a self-made millionaire known for extravagant parties attended by strangers who whisper rumors of his criminal past. Nick gradually learns that Gatsby’s entire fortune and mansion were acquired to rekindle a romance with Daisy, whom he loved five years earlier as a young officer before the war, when she married Tom Buchanan while he was away. Gatsby’s obsessive hope is centered on the green light across the bay, symbolizing his dream of recapturing the past.

As Nick grows closer to Gatsby, he learns the truth behind Gatsby’s origins: James Gatz, a poor North Dakota farm boy who reinvented himself after working for the wealthy Dan Cody and absorbing the trappings of high society. Gatsby’s fabricated history—Oxford, war heroism, inherited wealth—is exposed as carefully constructed myth, yet his emotional sincerity remains undeniable. When Nick arranges a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy at his own home, their rekindled passion is palpable, but Daisy’s hesitation reveals the impossibility of Gatsby’s dream. The tension escalates during a sweltering day in New York, where Gatsby confronts Tom in a hotel room; Daisy’s wavering declaration that she once loved Tom shatters Gatsby’s idealized vision. On the drive home, Daisy—driving Gatsby’s yellow car—accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, who mistakes the vehicle for Tom’s. Instead of taking responsibility, Tom manipulates George Wilson, Myrtle’s grief-stricken husband, into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer.

After the accident, Gatsby waits vigilantly outside Daisy’s house, determined to protect her, even as she retreats into the safety of Tom’s wealth. That night, George Wilson, consumed by delusion and manipulated by Tom, tracks Gatsby to his mansion and shoots him in the pool before turning the gun on himself. Nick, left to organize Gatsby’s funeral, finds that no one from the glittering crowd of partygoers attends—not even Meyer Wolfsheim or Klipspringer. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives, proud of his son’s rise but unaware of the corruption behind it. Nick confronts Jordan Baker, who ends their relationship, and encounters Tom on Fifth Avenue, where Tom coldly justifies his role in Gatsby’s death as self-defense. Disillusioned by the moral decay of the East, Nick returns to the Midwest, reflecting on Gatsby’s tragic belief that the past could be repeated. In the final moments, he watches the green light across the bay and contemplates humanity’s futile struggle against time: 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'
